headline: US markets took a hammering last night — NASDAQ down 5.5% on AI regulation fears after the midterms — but your ASX holdings held up relatively well today.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dropped sharply last night after a Reuters report revealed that AI data centre firm IREN is delaying Microsoft AI deliveries, raising doubts about the pace of its AI infrastructure buildout. Add in broader market panic over potential tighter AI regulation post-midterms, and tech stocks across the board got sold off hard.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS tracks the entire US share market, so last night's brutal NASDAQ and S&P 500 selloff (down 5.5% and 4.4% respectively) flowed straight through into today's ASX price. The catalyst was AI regulation fears following the US midterm results.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: An AI-focused ETF was always going to feel this one — chip stocks and AI data centre companies led the global selloff on fears that the new Congress will push for tighter rules on artificial intelligence. The fund fell 2.7% today on the ASX.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google fell nearly 2% last night as the broader tech selloff hit all the mega-caps. There's also an underlying structural worry doing the rounds — Bloomberg noted that Google's own AI products (like AI Overviews in Search) could cannibalise its core advertising revenue over time.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG holds a big chunk of international shares, so the overnight US market carnage dragged it down 1.6% today. Nothing specific to VDHG — it's just absorbing the global volatility.

movers.name: DHHF (BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF)
movers.note: Similar story to VDHG — DHHF is a globally diversified fund, so it tracked the international selloff. Down 1.5% today, mostly reflecting the US market moves overnight.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: A bright spot today — emerging markets actually rose 1.2%. The weaker Aussie dollar (down nearly 2% against the USD) boosts the AUD value of overseas holdings, and emerging market assets often attract some buying when investors rotate away from expensive US tech.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two bucked the trend last night, rising 2.1%. GTA 6 preorder sales reportedly hit $751 million with two weeks still to go before release, and the Take-Two CEO made bullish comments about their broader game library including Red Dead Redemption and Borderlands. The market liked it.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Flat day for Pilbara — no movement today. Lithium prices remain subdued, though there's a mild positive signal from Albemarle (a major US lithium producer) reporting a 58% rise in energy storage sales and a jump in adjusted earnings, suggesting demand is slowly recovering.

watch_today.title: AI regulation fears — your tech holdings in the crosshairs
watch_today.detail: The big story driving markets right now is fear that the new US Congress, following the midterm results, will push for tougher rules on artificial intelligence. That spooked chip stocks and AI-related shares globally — NASDAQ fell 5.5% last night, Japan's Nikkei briefly dived over 7%. Your GXAI.AX, MSFT, GOOG, VTS.AX and VDHG.AX all felt it. This may not be a one-day event — watch how this develops over coming days.

watch_today.title: MSFT — hold, don't panic on the AI infra delay news
watch_today.detail: Microsoft dropped 3.6% last night after reports that AI data centre partner IREN is delaying deliveries of Microsoft AI capacity. That's a real short-term headwind, but Microsoft's long-term AI story — cloud dominance, Copilot across Office, Azure growth — is very much intact. You're still up ~21% overall on this position. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — hold, the thesis is bruised but not broken
watch_today.detail: GXAI is your most underwater position (down 20% overall) and fell another 2.7% today as AI regulation fears hit the sector. It's painful, but selling now locks in the loss. The long-term case for AI as a growth theme is still very much alive — this is market noise, not a structural collapse of AI as a sector. Hold for the long term.

watch_today.title: TTWO — GTA 6 momentum building, hold confidently
watch_today.detail: Take-Two rose 2.1% last night and was one of the few winners in a brutal session. GTA 6 preorders have reportedly hit $751 million with two weeks to go before release — a massive commercial signal. The CEO also talked up their broader IP library. Your position is nearly back to even. Hold — the GTA 6 launch catalyst is right around the corner.

watch_today.title: RBA raised rates again — check your mortgage/savings
watch_today.detail: The Reserve Bank hiked the cash rate again in November. The RBA's deputy governor publicly admitted the bank is 'losing Australians' trust' on inflation. Savings account rates are rising (good for savers), but mortgage repayments are going up again. Worth checking if your savings account has been updated and reviewing any variable rate loans.

watch_today.title: VGE.AX — a rare green day, emerging markets holding up
watch_today.detail: Your Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF rose 1.2% today, bucking the global trend. Emerging markets can outperform when US tech is in trouble, as investors look elsewhere. The weaker Aussie dollar also flatters returns from overseas holdings. Nothing urgent — just a good sign that diversification is doing its job.

world.summary: The US midterm results are reshaping global politics and markets simultaneously — Republicans suffered a surprise loss partly blamed on the Iran war, oil tankers are being hit in the Strait of Hormuz, and AI regulation fears triggered one of the biggest tech selloffs in months.

stories.title: US midterms deliver shock result — Republicans blame Iran war for losses
stories.why_it_matters: Republicans lost control of Congress in the US midterms, with many in the party openly blaming Trump's decision to pursue war with Iran as the key factor. Vice President Vance walked a tightrope, criticising the Iran war strategy while trying not to directly attack Trump. With Trump now in a weakened 'lame-duck' position, there's growing uncertainty about US foreign policy — particularly in the Middle East. Financial Times reports the results will 'herald upheaval' in US Middle East policy.

stories.title: Oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as Iran keeps pressure on
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has attacked commercial tankers in the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow waterway through which about 20% of the world's oil passes — in the wake of the US midterm results. This is a direct escalation and keeps pressure on global oil prices. Crude oil ticked up slightly to $91.25/barrel. If the Strait were seriously disrupted, energy prices globally (including petrol at the pump for Aussies) would spike sharply.

stories.title: Iran reviewing 'concrete proposals' on its nuclear program
stories.why_it_matters: Despite the ongoing conflict, US officials say Iran is reviewing 'concrete proposals' regarding its nuclear program — a potential opening for diplomacy. This is a significant signal: if a deal were struck, it could reduce Middle East tensions and ease oil prices. But with Trump weakened domestically and Iran attacking tankers simultaneously, the path to any deal is very narrow.

stories.title: AI regulation fears trigger massive global market selloff
stories.why_it_matters: The US midterm result triggered a massive rethink about AI regulation, with investors fearing the new Congress will impose tighter rules on artificial intelligence companies and data centres. The NASDAQ fell 5.52% and the S&P 500 dropped 4.36% last night — one of the biggest single-day drops in years. Japan's Nikkei briefly plunged over 7% below 60,000. Chip stocks and AI data centre shares were hit hardest. This directly hammered your MSFT, GOOG, GXAI.AX, VTS.AX and VDHG.AX holdings.

stories.title: Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international football
stories.why_it_matters: Football legend Cristiano Ronaldo has announced his retirement from international football. The 41-year-old Portuguese superstar ends his international career as one of the most decorated players of all time, holding the record for most international goals. It's the end of an era for world football, closing the chapter on a rivalry with Messi that defined a generation of the sport.

markets.summary: Last night was ugly on Wall Street — the NASDAQ cratered 5.5% and the S&P 500 fell 4.4% on AI regulation fears post-midterms. The ASX held up relatively well today, slipping just 0.5%. Gold fell, oil ticked up slightly, and the Aussie dollar dropped nearly 2% — meaning your US holdings are worth a bit less when converted back to AUD.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Modest dip today — the ASX largely shrugged off the overnight US carnage, helped by defensive and resource stocks.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session. Massive drop driven by AI regulation fears after the US midterm results.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Last night's session. Tech and AI stocks led the selloff — one of the worst nights in recent memory for the index.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar fell sharply. This makes your US holdings (MSFT, GOOG, TTWO) worth less in AUD terms when converted back.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil ticked up slightly amid tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran attacked tankers overnight.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold fell — somewhat surprising given the market chaos. Investors may be selling gold to cover losses elsewhere.

politics.summary: It's a big week for Australia's economic story — the RBA hiked rates again, the central bank's deputy governor admitted it's 'losing public trust' on inflation, and Treasurer Chalmers is under pressure on wages, productivity and the federal budget.

stories.title: RBA hikes rates again in November — deputy governor admits trust is eroding
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank raised the cash rate again this month, pushing up mortgage repayments for Australians on variable rate loans. Savings account rates are rising in response — so check your bank has passed it on. More worrying: the RBA's deputy governor publicly conceded that the central bank is 'losing Australians' trust' to manage inflation — a rare and significant admission that the bank's credibility is under pressure after so many rate hikes.

stories.title: Chalmers under pressure on wages blowout and productivity
stories.why_it_matters: The federal government's own wage bill has blown out, putting more pressure on Treasurer Jim Chalmers to find budget savings. Meanwhile, Labor's productivity chief is publicly criticising the government's union-friendly industrial relations laws as a barrier to lifting productivity. Chalmers is now actively looking for ideas to boost productivity and rein in spending — suggesting a tighter budget is coming.

stories.title: Government warned over 'robodebt-style' risk with AI use
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government is being warned it risks repeating a 'robodebt-style' scandal by using algorithms and AI to make government decisions without adequate human oversight. Robodebt was a disastrous automated debt-recovery program that wrongly targeted welfare recipients and cost the government hundreds of millions in compensation. The warning comes as governments globally rush to use AI tools to cut costs — with serious risks if it goes wrong.

stories.title: AUKUS Bill gives sweeping powers to Defence Minister
stories.why_it_matters: New AUKUS legislation passing through Parliament gives the Defence Minister sweeping new powers to fast-track decisions related to the nuclear submarine deal. Critics say the bill concentrates too much authority in one minister with limited parliamentary oversight. The AUKUS submarine program is Australia's biggest-ever defence commitment — costing hundreds of billions of dollars over decades — so the governance arrangements matter a lot.

ai.summary: The biggest AI story today isn't a product launch — it's the market meltdown triggered by fears that the new US Congress will clamp down on artificial intelligence. Meanwhile, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Cyber and Tencent released a major open-source model.

stories.title: AI regulation fears torch tech stocks globally after US midterms
stories.why_it_matters: The US midterm results spooked investors into believing the new Congress will push for tighter rules on AI companies and the data centres they rely on. NASDAQ fell 5.5%, Japan's Nikkei briefly dived more than 7%, and AI-related stocks — from chip makers to cloud companies — led the global rout. This is the biggest single-day AI-related market event in recent memory, and it directly hit your GXAI.AX, MSFT, GOOG and VTS.AX holdings.

stories.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber — a security-focused AI model
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI has released GPT-6 Cyber, a new AI model specifically designed with cybersecurity in mind. The model is reportedly able to identify software flaws that hackers could exploit — meaning it can find security vulnerabilities before the bad guys do. This positions it as a competitor to Anthropic's Claude Mythos and Google's Gemini in the growing market for AI-powered security tools.

stories.title: Tencent launches Hy4 — joining the top tier of open-source AI models
stories.why_it_matters: Chinese tech giant Tencent has released Hy4, an open-source AI model it claims competes with the world's leading AI systems. 'Open-source' means anyone can download and use or modify it for free — a direct challenge to paid models like GPT and Claude. This continues the trend of Chinese tech companies releasing powerful AI models openly, increasing global competition and potentially driving down costs for businesses using AI tools.

stories.title: Australian government warned on AI use — robodebt echoes
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government is being warned it risks a 'robodebt 2.0' by deploying algorithms and AI to make government decisions without enough human checks. The original robodebt disaster wrongly sent hundreds of thousands of debt notices to welfare recipients and cost taxpayers over $1.8 billion in compensation and legal costs. The concern is that speed and cost-cutting pressures are pushing governments to automate decisions that need human judgment.

sport.summary: NRL Grand Final history was made last weekend with the Roosters edging the Knights 19-18 at Accor Stadium. Nathan Cleary faces another operation, Ronaldo calls time on international football, and Australia's surfers head to Peru targeting back-to-back World Surfing Championship gold.

stories.title: Roosters beat Knights 19-18 in Grand Final thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters won the NRL Grand Final last Sunday, defeating the Newcastle Knights by the narrowest possible margin — 19-18 at Accor Stadium. It was a heart-stopper of a game and the Roosters' championship is now confirmed. Knights fans will be gutted by the one-point loss on the biggest stage.

stories.title: Nathan Cleary facing another operation — Penrith's star at risk
stories.why_it_matters: Panthers star halfback Nathan Cleary is set to go under the knife again, raising serious concerns about his availability for the start of next season. Cleary is widely regarded as the best player in the NRL, and any extended absence would be a massive blow to Penrith's 2027 title hopes.

stories.title: Australia surfers head to Peru targeting back-to-back World Surfing gold
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's Irukandjis (national surfing team) are heading to Peru to compete in the World Surfing Championship, with the squad targeting back-to-back team gold medals. Australian surfing is riding high internationally, and a second consecutive title would cement the country's dominance in the sport.

stories.title: Ronaldo announces retirement from international football
stories.why_it_matters: Cristiano Ronaldo has officially retired from international football, ending a career with the Portuguese national team that produced a record number of international goals and multiple major tournament appearances. The 41-year-old signed off as one of the greatest footballers of all time, closing the curtain on the Ronaldo-vs-Messi era that captivated the world for two decades.

stories.title: Andreeva and Noskova — the new major champions bucking tennis tradition
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian Open is spotlighting two rising stars — Mirra Andreeva and Linda Noskova — as the new major champions reshaping women's tennis. Both players broke through at a young age, winning Grand Slam titles in a way that's unusual in the modern game dominated by experienced veterans. Worth watching as the Australian Open season builds toward January.
